plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two rose curves plotted on separate polar grids, set side by side and labeled (a) and (b) beneath. Each grid is built from dotted concentric circles crossed by dotted radial spokes, with solid horizontal and vertical axes arrowed at all four ends. Panel (a) holds a teal curve of eight identical petals, all springing from the origin at equal angular intervals so that four lie along the axes and four along the diagonals between them; its caption reads r = acos(n theta), n even. Panel (b) holds a curve in the same teal weight but with only three petals, one pointing straight down along the negative vertical axis and the other two angled up to the left and up to the right, spaced a third of a turn apart; its caption reads r = asin(n theta), n odd. Every petal reaches out to roughly the same radius, so each curve fills a circular envelope. Setting the panels side by side isolates the parity of n as the only thing governing the count: an even n produces 2n petals while an odd n produces just n, and the eight-petal and three-petal drawings are the two cases of that rule.

interactionPlan.concept: In a polar rose curve, the parity of the angular multiplier n determines the number of petals: 2n petals for an even n, and n petals for an odd n.
elements: Polar coordinate grid with dotted concentric circles
Dotted radial spoke lines at regular angular intervals
Solid horizontal x-axis with arrows at both ends
Solid vertical y-axis with arrows at both ends
Thick teal polar rose curve traced by the active equation
Dynamic equation label centered beneath the plot showing r = a f(nθ)

interactions.label: Multiplier (n)
interactions.teaches: An even n generates 2n petals because the curve requires a full 2π interval to close without overlapping, while an odd n completes the shape in just π, yielding exactly n petals.

interactions.label: Trig Function
interactions.teaches: Switching between cosine and sine rotates the entire curve by a fixed angle, changing its orientation but preserving the petal count.

interactions.label: Amplitude (a)
interactions.teaches: The factor 'a' defines the maximum radial distance of the petals, scaling the bounding circle without affecting the shape or petal count.

demo_steps.title: Even n
demo_steps.narration: When n is an even number, the rose has exactly 2n petals. Here, n=4 produces an 8-petal rose.

demo_steps.title: Odd n
demo_steps.narration: Change n to an odd number like 3. The curve now has exactly n (3) petals, because the graph traces back over itself during the second half of the 2π cycle.

demo_steps.title: Changing Orientation
demo_steps.narration: Switching the function to sine rotates the 3 petals to a new alignment, but the odd/even petal count rule remains exactly the same.

demo_steps.title: Changing Amplitude
demo_steps.narration: Shrinking the amplitude a shortens every petal, scaling the curve down without changing its underlying structural properties.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The geometry of a polar rose is independently controlled by three parts: 'a' dictates size, sine/cosine dictates rotation, and the parity (even/odd) of 'n' dictates the petal count.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Instead of drawing two static side-by-side panels like the original figure, render a single centralized dynamic polar plot that responds to the interactions. Draw background concentric circles and radial spokes in lightly visible dotted gray. Draw the main x/y axes as solid black lines with arrowheads at all extremities. Plot the rose curve as a bold, smooth teal path. Centered directly below the polar plot, display a dynamic text label (e.g., 'r = 4 cos(4θ)') matching the current UI state.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button/state for integer n: the learner steps through n values, the polar curve redraws with n petals for odd n and 2n petals for even n, making the parity rule visible instead of memorized.
- Toggle between cosine and sine forms: the learner switches r = a cos(n theta) and r = a sin(n theta), the rose rotates to a new orientation while the petal-count rule remains tied to n, separating orientation from parity.
- Slider for amplitude a: the learner changes a, every petal grows or shrinks to a new maximum radius without changing the number of petals, showing that a controls size rather than count.
- Equation input for the polar rose: learner edits r = a*cos(n*theta) or r = a*sin(n*theta), with fields for a and n; the graph redraws and petal count plus orientation update immediately.

authoredContext:
The formulas that generate the graph of a rose curve are given by r=acosnθ and r=asinnθ where a≠0. If n is even, the curve has 2n petals. If n is odd, the curve has n petals. See the figure.

Graph of two rose curves side by side. (A) is r=acos(ntheta), where n is even. Eight petals extending from origin, equally spaced. (B) is r=asin(ntheta) where n is odd. Three petals extending from the origin, equally spaced.

discrepancies: The equation label dynamically substitutes numeric values (e.g., 'r = 4cos(4θ)') instead of preserving the abstract symbolic parameters ('r = acos(nθ)') shown in the source.
The generated figure unifies the two static panels into a single interactive plot, omitting the '(a)' and '(b)' subfigure labels.
The radial grid lines are fixed at 45-degree intervals, whereas the source right panel adapts its grid to 30-degree intervals to match the 3-petal odd rose.
The condition text in the label adds the word 'is' ('n is even' instead of 'n even' / 'n odd').
The generated figure draws 5 concentric grid circles, while the source uses exactly 4.
evaluation.notes: An excellent interactive adaptation that successfully unifies the side-by-side static source plots into a single exploratory tool. The main deviations are minor hardcodings in the background grid and label text that don't match the source's exact presentation.
action_items: Update the drawn equation label to use the abstract variables 'a' and 'n' (i.e., 'r = acos(nθ), n even') to exactly match the source text, rather than dynamically printing the slider values.
Dynamically adapt the radial grid lines: use 30-degree (π/6) intervals when n=3 (or for odd numbers generally) to match how the source's second panel changes its grid to fit the 3-petal shape.
Remove the word 'is' from the parity label to match the source's concise 'n even' and 'n odd' formatting.
Reduce the number of concentric dotted grid circles from 5 to 4 to match the source figure.
